title: Service Mesh with Linkerd
summary: A service mesh adds a transparent proxy layer to all service-to-service traffic, giving you mutual TLS, retries, timeouts, circuit breaking, and rich observability — without changing a single line of application code. Linkerd is the CNCF-graduated lightweight option for Kubernetes; Istio adds more features at the cost of significant operational complexity.

sections.title: What problem does a service mesh solve?
sections.body:
## The Problem That Service Meshes Solve

When a system is a single monolith, cross-cutting concerns like encryption, retries, and observability can be added once in a shared library or middleware layer. When that system is split into dozens of microservices — each potentially written in a different language, owned by a different team — those same concerns must be re-implemented in every service, consistently, and kept in sync as requirements evolve.

This is the coordination problem that a **service mesh** solves. Rather than encoding network reliability logic in application code, a service mesh externalizes it into a dedicated infrastructure layer. Every service gets a lightweight **sidecar proxy** automatically injected alongside it. All network traffic the service sends or receives passes through this proxy. The proxy enforces policies, collects metrics, handles retries, and terminates TLS — none of which requires a single line of application code to change.

From a DevOps perspective, this is transformative in three ways:

**Security:** mTLS between every pair of services becomes the default, not an opt-in feature individual teams might skip. Each service has a cryptographic identity issued by the mesh's certificate authority. You can write authorization policy based on identity — "only the orders service is allowed to call the payments service" — and the mesh enforces it at the network level.

**Reliability:** timeouts, retries, and circuit breakers are configured centrally using Kubernetes resources, not scattered across service configuration files in five different languages. A platform team can enforce a standard retry budget cluster-wide.

**Observability:** because every request passes through the proxy, the mesh can emit consistent latency, throughput, and error rate metrics for every service pair — the so-called "golden signals" — without instrumentation in application code. Distributed traces can be propagated automatically.

As microservices scale, you need consistent answers to these questions for **every** service:

```
Security:      Is traffic between Service A and B encrypted?
               How do I know Service B is really who it says it is?

Reliability:   What happens when Service B is slow?
               Should we retry failed requests?
               Should we circuit-break when B is down?

Observability: How long did that call take?
               What is the error rate between A and B?
               Which service caused this request to be slow?
```

**Without a service mesh, each team implements this separately:**

```python
# Every service adds this boilerplate:
import requests
from tenacity import retry, stop_after_attempt, wait_exponential

@retry(stop=stop_after_attempt(3), wait=wait_exponential(min=1, max=10))
def call_inventory_service(item_id):
    try:
        resp = requests.get(
            f"https://inventory-service/api/items/{item_id}",
            timeout=5,
            verify=CERT_PATH    # each team manages their own certs
        )
        resp.raise_for_status()
        return resp.json()
    except Exception as e:
        metrics.increment("inventory_call_errors")  # each team instruments separately
        raise
```

**With a service mesh, the proxy handles it transparently:**

```
Your application code:
    response = requests.get("http://inventory-service/api/items/123")
    # Plain HTTP, no retries, no TLS code, no metrics

The sidecar proxy (Linkerd or Envoy) transparently:
    ✓ Upgrades to mTLS (encrypts + authenticates the connection)
    ✓ Retries on connection failures
    ✓ Times out after configured duration
    ✓ Records latency, error rate as Prometheus metrics
    ✓ Adds trace spans to every call
    ✓ Circuit-breaks if error rate exceeds threshold
```

**The sidecar pattern:**

```
Pod: my-app
  Container 1: my-app           (your code)
  Container 2: linkerd-proxy    (injected by mesh, handles all network I/O)

All traffic in/out of the pod goes through the proxy.
The proxy is completely transparent to the application.
Injection is automatic: label namespace → all new pods get the sidecar.
```

sections.title: Linkerd vs Istio
sections.body:
## Choosing a Service Mesh: Linkerd vs Istio

The two dominant CNCF-graduated service meshes — Linkerd and Istio — both solve the same fundamental problem but make very different tradeoffs. Choosing between them is not primarily a technical decision; it is an **organizational and operational capacity decision**.

Istio is built on the [Envoy proxy](https://www.envoyproxy.io/), which is one of the most capable network proxies ever built. Its feature set is exhaustive: fine-grained traffic control, WebAssembly plugin extensibility, external authorization integrations, multi-cluster topologies, and more. That power comes with complexity — Istio adds 50+ CRDs to your cluster, has historically been difficult to upgrade safely, and its configuration surface area is large enough that misconfiguration is a common source of outages. Organizations that choose Istio typically have a dedicated platform engineering team whose job is to operate the mesh.

Linkerd takes the opposite philosophy. Its proxy is written in Rust (not C++ like Envoy), which means it is small, fast, and memory-safe by design. Linkerd deliberately omits features it considers out of scope — there is no rate limiting plugin, no WebAssembly extension point, no external auth — in exchange for dramatically reduced operational burden. Installation, upgrades, and day-to-day operation are straightforward. For most organizations that simply want mTLS everywhere and golden metrics without a dedicated mesh team, Linkerd is the right choice.

This lesson uses Linkerd because the sandbox cluster is resource-constrained and because Linkerd's operational simplicity makes it a better teaching tool. The concepts — sidecar injection, mTLS, traffic policy, ServiceProfile — transfer directly to Istio if your organization uses it; only the specific CRD names and annotation keys differ.

**Linkerd** — Rust-based, ultra-lightweight, CNCF graduated.

```
Pros:
  - Tiny resource footprint (~10MB RAM per proxy)
  - Simple installation and operation
  - Automatic mTLS with zero-config
  - Strong default security posture
  - Excellent Prometheus/Grafana integration
  - Fast: written in Rust (not Go/C++)

Cons:
  - Less feature-rich than Istio
  - No Envoy (some features require Envoy ecosystem)
  - Traffic management less granular than Istio's

Best for:
  - Teams that want security and observability with low ops overhead
  - Organizations that need mTLS everywhere without complexity
  - k3s/edge deployments where resources are constrained
```

**Istio** — Envoy-based, feature-rich, CNCF graduated.

```
Pros:
  - Extremely granular traffic control
  - VirtualService, DestinationRule, EnvoyFilter CRDs
  - Rich ecosystem (Kiali, Jaeger integration)
  - Multi-cluster support
  - External authorization (OPA, custom)

Cons:
  - Heavy resource usage (Istiod + per-pod Envoy proxies)
  - Complex configuration (many CRDs, easy to misconfigure)
  - Historically difficult upgrades
  - Steep learning curve

Best for:
  - Organizations that need fine-grained traffic control
  - Multi-cluster topologies
  - Teams with dedicated platform/mesh expertise
```

**Quick comparison:**

```
Feature              Linkerd         Istio
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
mTLS                 auto            auto
Retries              yes             yes
Circuit breaking     yes             yes
Traffic splitting    yes             yes (more granular)
Header-based routing limited         yes
Rate limiting        no              yes (via EnvoyFilter)
External authz       no              yes
Proxy                linkerd2-proxy  Envoy
Proxy memory (idle)  ~10MB           ~50-150MB
Install complexity   low             high
CRDs added           ~15             ~50+
```

sections.title: Installing Linkerd on Kubernetes
sections.body:
## Installing Linkerd: What Actually Happens

Linkerd has two main components: the **CLI** (a local tool for interacting with the mesh) and the **control plane** (a set of Kubernetes deployments that manage certificate issuance, proxy configuration, and the metrics pipeline).

The control plane runs in the `linkerd` namespace and consists of three core components:

| Component | Role |
|---|---|
| **linkerd-destination** | Serves proxy configuration (endpoints, load balancing, policy) |
| **linkerd-identity** | Issues mTLS certificates to proxies (acts as the mesh CA) |
| **linkerd-proxy-injector** | Mutating admission webhook that injects the sidecar into new pods |

The injection mechanism is worth understanding in detail. When you annotate a namespace with `linkerd.io/inject=enabled`, the proxy injector registers itself as a Kubernetes **mutating admission webhook**. Every time a pod is created in that namespace, Kubernetes sends the pod spec to the injector before persisting it. The injector adds the `linkerd-proxy` container, an init container that sets up iptables rules, and the necessary volume mounts — then returns the modified spec. From Kubernetes' perspective, the pod always had two containers; it never sees the un-injected version.

This is why you must **restart existing deployments** after annotating a namespace. The webhook only fires on pod creation — pods already running were created before the annotation was applied and will not have the sidecar unless restarted.

The `linkerd check --pre` command validates cluster prerequisites before installation: kernel version, available APIs, existing CRD conflicts. Running it first saves significant debugging time on non-standard cluster configurations.

**Install Linkerd CLI:**

```bash norun
# Install the CLI
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSfL https://run.linkerd.io/install | sh
export PATH=$PATH:$HOME/.linkerd2/bin

# Verify version
linkerd version

# Check if your cluster is ready for Linkerd
linkerd check --pre
```

**Install Linkerd control plane:**

```bash norun
# Generate install manifests and apply
linkerd install --crds | kubectl apply -f -
linkerd install | kubectl apply -f -

# Wait for it to be ready
linkerd check

# Install the viz extension (Prometheus + Grafana + dashboard)
linkerd viz install | kubectl apply -f -
linkerd check

# Open the dashboard
linkerd viz dashboard &
# http://localhost:50750
```

**Inject the mesh into a namespace or deployment:**

```bash norun
# Option 1: annotate a namespace (all new pods get injected)
kubectl annotate namespace default linkerd.io/inject=enabled

# Then redeploy to pick up the sidecar:
kubectl rollout restart deployment/web-app

# Option 2: inject into a specific deployment
kubectl get deploy web-app -o yaml | linkerd inject - | kubectl apply -f -

# Verify injection
linkerd check --proxy -n default
kubectl get pods -n default -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{" "}{.spec.containers[*].name}{"\n"}{end}'
# You should see: web-app-xxx  web-app linkerd-proxy
```

**Linkerd resources created per-namespace:**

```yaml
# Linkerd adds these annotations to pods after injection:
annotations:
  linkerd.io/inject: enabled
  linkerd.io/proxy-version: stable-2.14.0
  config.linkerd.io/proxy-cpu-request: "100m"
  config.linkerd.io/proxy-memory-request: "20Mi"

# And these env vars to the sidecar:
# LINKERD2_PROXY_DESTINATION_SVC_ADDR  — control plane address
# LINKERD2_PROXY_IDENTITY_TRUST_ANCHORS — root CA cert for mTLS
```

sections.title: Traffic management and mesh observability
sections.body:
## Traffic Management and Observability in Linkerd

Once the Linkerd proxy is injected into your pods, you gain two categories of capability: **traffic management** (telling the proxy how to handle requests) and **observability** (reading what the proxy reports about traffic it has seen).

**Traffic management** in Linkerd is configured through `ServiceProfile` resources (Linkerd's own CRD) and the newer `HTTPRoute` CRD from the Gateway API. A `ServiceProfile` lets you define per-route behavior: which HTTP status codes count as failures, how long to wait before timing out, and how aggressively to retry. This is important because the proxy cannot know your application's semantics by itself — a `404` response from a search API might be a successful "not found" result, not an error that should be retried.

The **retry budget** concept is central to safe retry configuration. Naive retry logic can cause **retry storms**: if 1000 requests fail and each is retried 3 times, the backend suddenly receives 4000 requests when it is already struggling. Linkerd's retry budget uses a ratio (e.g., 0.2 = 20% of requests can be retries) rather than a fixed retry count, so retries scale with actual traffic volume and back off automatically when the backend is overwhelmed.

**Observability** comes from the Prometheus metrics the proxy emits automatically. The "golden signals" — request rate, error rate, and latency percentiles — are available for every deployment without any application instrumentation. The `linkerd viz` commands provide a CLI-native view of these metrics, and the built-in Grafana dashboards show them visually. The `linkerd viz tap` command is particularly powerful during incident response: it shows a live stream of actual HTTP requests flowing through a deployment, including path, status code, and latency — equivalent to real-time access logging without touching the application.

**Linkerd traffic management (HTTPRoute / ServiceProfile):**

```yaml
# ServiceProfile: define retries and timeouts per-route
apiVersion: linkerd.io/v1alpha2
kind: ServiceProfile
metadata:
  name: web-app.default.svc.cluster.local
  namespace: default
spec:
  routes:
  - name: GET /api/orders/{id}
    condition:
      method: GET
      pathRegex: /api/orders/[^/]+
    responseClasses:
    - condition:
        status:
          min: 500
          max: 599
      isFailure: true
    timeout: 10s
    retryBudget:
      retryRatio: 0.2        # retry up to 20% of requests
      minRetriesPerSecond: 10
      ttl: 10s
```

**Linkerd golden metrics (auto, without code changes):**

```bash norun
# After injecting your app, these metrics appear automatically in Prometheus:

# Success rate (% of requests that succeeded)
linkerd_request_total{direction="inbound", tls="true"}  

# Latency percentiles
linkerd_request_duration_ms_bucket{..., le="50"}

# In PromQL:
sum(rate(response_total{namespace="default", deployment="web-app", classification="success"}[1m]))
/
sum(rate(response_total{namespace="default", deployment="web-app"}[1m]))

# CLI: live golden metrics
linkerd viz stat deployments -n default
linkerd viz top deployment/web-app -n default
linkerd viz tap deployment/web-app -n default  # live request stream
```

**Automatic mTLS — verify encryption:**

```bash norun
# Show mTLS status for all connections
linkerd viz edges deployment -n default
# Output:
# SRC            DST            SRC_NS    DST_NS    SECURED
# web-app        api-server     default   learning  √
# prometheus     web-app        monitoring default  √

# All √ means all connections are encrypted with mTLS
# Linkerd handles certificate rotation automatically (every 24h)
```

**Traffic splitting (canary deployments):**

```yaml
# Split traffic 90/10 between stable and canary
apiVersion: split.smi-spec.io/v1alpha1
kind: TrafficSplit
metadata:
  name: web-app-canary
  namespace: default
spec:
  service: web-app
  backends:
  - service: web-app-stable
    weight: 900m    # 90%
  - service: web-app-canary
    weight: 100m    # 10%
```

sections.title: Exercise: install Linkerd in the sandbox
sections.body:
## Exercise: Standing Up a Real Service Mesh

This exercise walks through the full Linkerd installation lifecycle on the k3s sandbox cluster. The goal is not just to get Linkerd running, but to develop the muscle memory for the verification steps that tell you whether the mesh is actually working — because a mesh that is installed but not injecting, or injected but not enforcing mTLS, provides false security.

The workflow follows the natural order of a real deployment:

1. **Pre-flight validation** — check that the cluster meets Linkerd's requirements before installing anything. This avoids wasting time on an install that will partially fail.
2. **Control plane installation** — CRDs first (they define the API), then the control plane components. Separating these two `apply` calls matches how Linkerd documents upgrades.
3. **Injection** — you will inject a specific deployment rather than the whole namespace, to see the injection mechanism up close.
4. **Verification** — the `linkerd check` commands are your go-to health checks. Learn to read their output; each check maps to a specific control plane component.
5. **Observability** — viewing golden metrics and mTLS status confirms the mesh is actually doing work, not just running idle.

If `linkerd check --pre` reports failures in the sandbox, read each failure carefully. Some (like `ClusterRole` permission gaps) are environment constraints; others (like kernel version) indicate genuine incompatibilities. The pre-flight output is designed to be actionable — each failure includes a URL with remediation steps.

Install Linkerd in the k3s sandbox and inject a sample deployment.

```bash norun
# ── 1. Install Linkerd CLI ────────────────────────────────────────────────
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSfL https://run.linkerd.io/install | sh
export PATH=$PATH:/root/.linkerd2/bin
linkerd version --client

# ── 2. Pre-flight check ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
linkerd check --pre
# Note any failures — some may be expected in the sandbox

# ── 3. Install CRDs and control plane ────────────────────────────────────
linkerd install --crds | kubectl apply -f -
linkerd install | kubectl apply -f -

# Watch the control plane come up:
kubectl get pods -n linkerd -w

# ── 4. Verify installation ────────────────────────────────────────────────
linkerd check

# ── 5. Inject the web-app deployment ─────────────────────────────────────
kubectl get deploy web-app -o yaml | linkerd inject - | kubectl apply -f -
kubectl rollout status deploy/web-app

# Confirm the sidecar was injected:
kubectl describe pod -l app=web-app | grep -A3 'linkerd-proxy'

# ── 6. View golden metrics ────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Generate some traffic first:
for i in $(seq 1 10); do
  kubectl exec -n default deploy/web-app -- wget -qO- localhost/ 2>/dev/null || true
done

# View stats:
linkerd viz stat deploy -n default

# ── 7. Explore mTLS status ────────────────────────────────────────────────
linkerd viz edges deploy -n default

# ── 8. Check what Linkerd metrics are in Prometheus ──────────────────────
# Port-forward Prometheus:
kubectl port-forward svc/monitoring-prometheus -n monitoring 9090:9090 &
echo "Prometheus at http://localhost:9090"

# In Prometheus UI, query:
# linkerd_request_total
# This shows per-deployment request totals with success/failure classification

# ── 9. View in the Linkerd dashboard (if viz is installed) ───────────────
# linkerd viz install | kubectl apply -f -
# linkerd viz dashboard &
# http://localhost:50750
```

questions.q: What is the sidecar pattern in the context of a service mesh?
options: A secondary container in the same pod that intercepts all network traffic on behalf of the main application container
A dedicated node running the mesh control plane
A load balancer that sits in front of all services
An init container that configures iptables rules
questions.explanation: The sidecar proxy is a second container injected into every pod alongside the application container. It intercepts all inbound and outbound network traffic (via iptables rules) and handles TLS, retries, metrics, and tracing transparently — without application code changes.

questions.q: Which of the following does Linkerd provide automatically after mesh injection, without any code changes?
options: Mutual TLS, request latency metrics, and success rate per deployment
questions.explanation: After injecting the Linkerd proxy, you get automatic mTLS for all meshed traffic, and the proxy emits Prometheus metrics for success rate, request latency (p50/p95/p99), and requests per second — for every deployment, without any application code changes.

questions.q: A ServiceProfile with a retryBudget of retryRatio: 0.2 means:
options: Each request is retried up to 2 times
Up to 20% of requests can be retried without causing budget exhaustion
Retries are disabled for 20% of requests
questions.explanation: The retryBudget retryRatio controls the ratio of retries to original requests. A value of 0.2 means retries can account for up to 20% of total traffic. This prevents retry storms — if the backend is slow, you won't amplify the load with excessive retries.

sections.title: Challenge: verify mTLS and inspect live traffic
sections.goal: With Linkerd installed, inject the 'api-server' deployment in the learning namespace, generate traffic between web-app and api-server, then use linkerd viz to verify that the connection is secured with mTLS and capture a live request stream showing the HTTP calls.
hints: Annotate the learning namespace: kubectl annotate namespace learning linkerd.io/inject=enabled
Restart deployments to pick up injection: kubectl rollout restart deploy -n learning
Generate traffic with: kubectl exec -n default deploy/web-app -- wget -qO- api-server.learning.svc.cluster.local:8080
Use: linkerd viz edges deploy -n default to see mTLS status
Use: linkerd viz tap deploy/web-app -n default to stream live requests
success_criteria: The api-server pod in learning namespace shows 2 containers (including linkerd-proxy)
linkerd viz edges shows a SECURED (√) connection between web-app and api-server
linkerd viz stat deploy -n learning shows success rate > 0%
linkerd viz tap produces live output showing HTTP/2 requests
